title: Atom-selective spin-polarized transport in a charge-ordered altermagnet
authors: Liu Yang, Yuan-Yuan Jiang, Xiao-Yan Guo, Yi-Dong Liu, Xian-Zhe Chen, Wen-Jian Lu, Yu-Ping Sun, Ming Li, Ding-Fu Shao
abstract: Altermagnets provide a promising platform for spin-polarized transport without net magnetization, but their transport properties are usually discussed in terms of momentum-space spin splitting. Here, using first-principles calculations and quantum transport simulations, we show that the charge-ordered altermagnet $α$-Fe$_2$PO$_5$ exhibits a distinct form of real-space spin selectivity despite weak altermagnetic spin splitting near the Fermi level. The charge order creates inequivalent Fe$^{2+}$ and Fe$^{3+}$ sites within each sublattice, while the puckered C-type antiferromagnetic stacking suppresses inter-sublattice transport. As a result, electron and hole doping activate spin-polarized transport predominantly through Fe$^{3+}$- and Fe$^{2+}$-based channels, respectively. These atom-selective channels carry opposite spin polarizations on the two antiferromagnetic sublattices, giving rise to a globally compensated charge current with hidden Néel spin character. We further propose an all-in-one $α$-Fe$_2$PO$_5$ tunnel junction, where matching or mismatching atom-selective conduction channels yields orders-of-magnitude conductance modulation. Our findings establish a real-space design principle for atomically controlled spin functionality and spintronic devices.
summary: This work analyzes spin-polarized transport in the altermagnet $\alpha$-Fe$_2$PO$_5$, demonstrating that charge ordering induces a real-space, atom-selective mechanism for spin current flow despite weak bulk magnetic splitting. By modeling an all-in-one tunnel junction, the authors show that controlling the atomic conduction channels—rather than just momentum overlap—allows for massive modulation of spin conductance.
main_problem: To investigate spin-polarized transport in altermagnets by moving beyond conventional momentum-space descriptions to focus on real-space electronic selectivity.
main_result: The charge-ordered altermagnet $\alpha$-Fe$_2$PO$_5$ exhibits atom-selective spin-polarized transport, allowing for orders-of-magnitude conductance modulation in a tunnel junction based on matching or mismatching atomic conduction channels.
method: First-principles calculations (DFT) combined with quantum transport simulations using the Non-Equilibrium Green's Function (NEGF) formalism.
model_or_system: The physical system is $\alpha$-Fe$_2$PO$_5$, a charge-ordered altermagnet characterized by inequivalent Fe$^{2+}$ and Fe$^{3+}$ sites within its sublattices, which dictates the spin-selective transport pathways.
key_observables: Spin-polarized current flow pathways, local conductance modulation ($\mathcal{T}_{ij}^{\sigma}$), and ON/OFF switching ratios in a tunnel junction.
important_parameters: Weak altermagnetic spin splitting near $E_F$; doping energy ($E_{n}^s, E_{p}^s$); lattice structure details (puckered C-type stacking).
main_assumptions: The standard momentum-space description fails to capture the crucial role of local and atomically-resolved electronic states in determining transport.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate crystal structures, band/DOS calculations showing site-resolved features, constant-energy surfaces confirming weak splitting, and real-space bond-resolved transmission ($\mathcal{T}_{ij}^{\sigma}$) for different doping configurations in a tunnel junction schematic.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from establishing the limitations of momentum-space analysis to demonstrating atom-selective transport via site-specific channels (Fe$^{3+}$ vs Fe$^{2+}$) and culminates in proposing an all-in-one tunnel junction where real-space channel matching controls conductance modulation.
why_interesting: While focused on solid-state magnetism, the concept of controlling quantum transport through engineered atomic connectivity and valence states has parallels with designing controlled coupling elements in superconducting or molecular quantum circuits.
